title: Storage Accounts, Encryption & Data Tools
summary: Choose the right storage account type and performance tier, configure encryption and object replication, and move data with AzCopy and Storage Explorer.
overview: A storage account is the top-level namespace for Azure Storage data: blobs, files, queues and tables. Its name is globally unique and forms endpoints such as https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net.

The account kind and performance tier decide which services and redundancy options you get. Standard general-purpose v2 is the default choice for most scenarios. Premium accounts use SSDs for low latency and come in specific flavors: block blobs, file shares, or page blobs.
All data is encrypted at rest automatically with Storage Service Encryption (256-bit AES). You can use Microsoft-managed keys (default) or customer-managed keys in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM.

keyConcepts.definition: Supports blobs (including Data Lake Gen2), files, queues and tables with all redundancy options. Recommended for most workloads.
SSD-backed accounts for high transaction rates and low latency with block and append blobs.
SSD-backed account (FileStorage) for Azure Files; supports SMB and NFS shares.
SSD-backed page blobs (used for unmanaged disks and some specialized workloads).
You control the encryption key in Key Vault; the account needs a managed identity with access to the key.
Optional second layer of encryption at the infrastructure level; must be enabled when the account is created.
Asynchronously copies block blobs from a source container to a destination container in another account. Requires blob versioning on both accounts and change feed on the source.
Command-line tool for high-performance copy/sync to and from Azure Storage, authenticating with Entra ID or SAS.
Free desktop GUI for managing blobs, files, queues and tables across accounts.

howItWorks: Create the account in a resource group, pick a region, performance (Standard/Premium), redundancy and, for Premium, the account type.
Configure networking (public access, firewall, private endpoints), data protection (soft delete, versioning) and encryption options.
Applications reach data through service endpoints for blob, file, queue, table and dfs, authenticated with Entra ID, shared keys or SAS.
For bulk data movement, use AzCopy (scriptable) or Storage Explorer (GUI); for offline transfers of very large datasets, Azure Data Box.
For cross-account copies of new and updated block blobs, configure an object replication policy.
whenToUse: Use Standard GPv2 unless you have a specific need for premium performance.
Use Premium block blobs for IoT, analytics or interactive workloads with many small transactions.
Use Premium file shares for latency-sensitive SMB/NFS workloads, such as databases or high-performance file servers.
Use object replication to reduce read latency in another region or to distribute data for processing.
examTips: Premium storage accounts support only LRS and ZRS redundancy — no geo-redundancy.
Infrastructure (double) encryption can only be enabled at account creation.
Object replication needs blob versioning enabled on both accounts and change feed on the source; it works with block blobs.
AzCopy 'sync' copies only changed files; 'copy' copies everything specified.
The storage account name must be globally unique, 3–24 characters, lowercase letters and numbers only.
commonMistakes: Choosing a legacy account kind (GPv1 or BlobStorage) for new workloads.
Expecting to switch an existing account from Standard to Premium — performance tier can't be changed after creation; migrate data instead.
Forgetting to grant the account's managed identity access to the Key Vault key when enabling CMK.

confusedWith.name: Managed disks
confusedWith.difference: VM disks are managed disks — you don't place them in a storage account you manage.

confusedWith.name: Azure Files vs Blob storage
confusedWith.difference: Both live in a storage account; Files offers SMB/NFS shares, Blob offers object storage over HTTPS.

title: Storage Redundancy: LRS, ZRS, GRS, GZRS
summary: How Azure Storage keeps copies of your data within a datacenter, across zones, and across regions — and what each option protects against.
overview: Azure Storage always stores multiple copies of your data. The redundancy option decides where those copies live, which determines what failures you survive.

In the primary region, data is replicated three times either within a single datacenter (LRS) or across three availability zones (ZRS). Geo-redundant options (GRS, GZRS) additionally copy data asynchronously to a paired secondary region, where it's stored with LRS.

By default, the secondary copy is not readable. Read-access variants (RA-GRS, RA-GZRS) expose a secondary endpoint (<account>-secondary) so applications can read during a primary outage. If the primary region is lost, a failover makes the secondary the new primary.

keyConcepts.definition: Three synchronous copies within one datacenter in the primary region. Protects against drive/rack failure; not against a datacenter or zone outage.
Three synchronous copies across three availability zones in the primary region. Data stays available if a zone fails.
LRS in the primary region plus asynchronous copy to the secondary region (also LRS there).
ZRS in the primary region plus asynchronous copy to the secondary region (LRS there). Highest durability and availability.
Adds read access to the secondary region's endpoint at all times.
You can initiate failover of a geo-redundant account to the secondary region. Because replication is asynchronous, recent writes may be lost (RPO > 0).
Property indicating the most recent time data is guaranteed to be on the secondary — helps estimate potential data loss.

howItWorks: Writes are committed synchronously to the three primary copies (LRS or ZRS) before success is returned.
For geo options, data is then copied asynchronously to the secondary region (typically within minutes, no SLA on replication lag).
With RA- options, apps can read from the secondary endpoint, which may lag the primary.
In a regional outage, Microsoft or the customer can fail over; after failover the account becomes LRS in the new primary until you reconfigure geo-redundancy.
whenToUse: LRS: cheapest option for data you can reconstruct or that has other copies, or where data residency forbids leaving a region.
ZRS: high availability within a region, e.g., for apps that must survive a zone outage.
GRS / RA-GRS: protection against a full regional disaster; RA if apps must read during an outage.
GZRS / RA-GZRS: critical data requiring both zone resilience and regional disaster protection.
examTips: 'Survive a datacenter/zone failure' → ZRS (or GZRS). 'Survive a regional outage' → GRS/GZRS. 'Read during regional outage' → RA-GRS/RA-GZRS.
Premium storage accounts (block blob, file share, page blob) support only LRS and ZRS.
The secondary copy in GRS/GZRS is always LRS in the secondary region.
The Archive access tier is supported only on LRS, GRS and RA-GRS accounts — not ZRS-based options.
Changing between some redundancy types (e.g., LRS→ZRS) requires a conversion or migration rather than a simple setting change, depending on the account.
commonMistakes: Thinking GRS lets you read from the secondary without failover — that requires RA-GRS.
Assuming geo-replication is synchronous (zero data loss). It is asynchronous.
Choosing ZRS when the requirement is to survive the loss of an entire region.

confusedWith.name: Azure Backup
confusedWith.difference: Redundancy protects against hardware and site failures; it faithfully replicates deletions and corruption. Backups (and soft delete/versioning) protect against accidental deletion.

confusedWith.name: Object replication
confusedWith.difference: Object replication copies selected containers to another account you choose; geo-redundancy replicates the whole account to the paired region automatically.

docLinks.title: Azure storage disaster recovery planning and failover
Change how a storage account is replicated

versionNote: Feature support by redundancy type (for example, archive tier and conversion options) has changed over time. Check the redundancy documentation for current support.

title: Blob Storage, Access Tiers & Lifecycle Management
summary: Containers and blob types, Hot/Cool/Cold/Archive tiers, lifecycle rules, versioning and soft delete.
overview: Azure Blob Storage is object storage for unstructured data — documents, images, video, backups, logs. Data is stored as blobs inside containers in a storage account and accessed over HTTPS.

Access tiers trade storage cost against access cost. Hot is cheapest to access and most expensive to store; Archive is cheapest to store but offline — blobs must be rehydrated before they can be read.

Lifecycle management policies automatically move blobs to cooler tiers or delete them based on age or last access, and data protection features (soft delete, versioning, point-in-time restore) guard against accidental deletion and overwrite.

keyConcepts.definition: For text and binary objects up to very large sizes; the default for most files.
Optimized for append operations such as logging.
Random read/write 512-byte pages; backs VHDs.
Private (default), Blob (anonymous read of blobs) or Container (anonymous read and list). Can be blocked account-wide by disallowing anonymous access.
Frequently accessed data. Highest storage cost, lowest access cost.
Infrequently accessed data kept at least 30 days; early-deletion charge applies before then.
Rarely accessed data kept at least 90 days, still online.
Offline storage for data kept at least 180 days. Reads require rehydration to an online tier, which can take hours (standard priority up to ~15 hours).
JSON rules with filters (prefix, blob type, index tags) and actions (tier to cool/cold/archive, delete) based on days since modification, creation or last access.
Automatically keeps previous versions when a blob is overwritten or deleted.
Retains deleted blobs or containers for a retention period (1–365 days) so they can be restored.

howItWorks: Create a container, set its access level, and upload blobs. The account default access tier (Hot or Cool; newer accounts may also allow Cold) applies to blobs without an explicit tier.
Set a tier per blob, or let a lifecycle policy move blobs automatically. Lifecycle policies run roughly once a day, so actions are not instantaneous.
To read an archived blob, rehydrate it by changing its tier to Hot/Cool/Cold or copying it to an online tier; choose standard or high priority.
Enable soft delete (blob and container), versioning and optionally point-in-time restore to protect against accidental changes.
whenToUse: Hot: active data such as web content or data being processed.
Cool: short-term backups and older data accessed occasionally.
Cold: data retained for months that must remain immediately readable.
Archive: long-term retention and compliance data that can tolerate hours of retrieval latency.
Lifecycle management: any time data predictably cools with age.
examTips: 'Minimize storage cost for data rarely accessed, retrieval within hours acceptable' → Archive. 'Must be available immediately' → Cool or Cold, never Archive.
Moving or deleting a blob before its tier's minimum days incurs an early deletion charge (Cool 30, Cold 90, Archive 180).
Lifecycle rules using last access time require access time tracking to be enabled.
Archive isn't available on ZRS, GZRS or RA-GZRS accounts.
Soft delete protects against deletion; versioning protects against overwrites; both can be combined.
To prevent anonymous access across an account, disable 'Allow Blob anonymous access' on the storage account.
commonMistakes: Expecting an archived blob to be readable immediately.
Assuming lifecycle policies act the moment the age threshold is reached.
Setting the account default tier to Archive (not allowed — Archive is set per blob).
Confusing container soft delete with blob soft delete — they're separate settings.

confusedWith.name: Azure Files
confusedWith.difference: Blob storage is object storage over HTTPS/REST; Azure Files provides SMB/NFS file shares you can mount.

confusedWith.name: Storage redundancy
confusedWith.difference: Tiers decide cost vs access latency; redundancy decides how many copies and where.

versionNote: Tier minimum retention periods, rehydration times and tier availability can change; confirm on Microsoft Learn.

title: Azure Files & Azure File Sync
summary: Fully managed SMB/NFS file shares, identity-based access, snapshots and soft delete, and syncing on-premises file servers with Azure File Sync.
overview: Azure Files offers fully managed file shares that can be mounted over SMB (Windows, Linux, macOS) or NFS (Linux, premium shares). Shares replace or extend on-premises file servers and support lift-and-shift apps that expect a file system.

Access can use the storage account key, or identity-based authentication over SMB with on-premises AD DS, Microsoft Entra Domain Services, or Microsoft Entra Kerberos for hybrid identities. Share-level permissions come from Azure RBAC roles; file- and folder-level permissions from Windows ACLs.
Azure File Sync caches Azure file shares on Windows Servers. Cloud tiering keeps frequently accessed files local and replaces cold files with pointers, so a small server can front a large share.

keyConcepts.definition: SMB mounts require outbound TCP 445, which many ISPs and corporate networks block — use VPN, ExpressRoute or Azure File Sync instead.
Storage File Data SMB Share Reader, Contributor and Elevated Contributor grant share access to identities.
Read-only, point-in-time, incremental copy of a share; up to 200 per share. Users can restore files via Previous Versions.
Deleted shares are retained for a configurable period (1–365 days) and can be undeleted.
The top-level Azure resource for Azure File Sync.
Defines the sync topology: exactly one cloud endpoint (an Azure file share) and one or more server endpoints.
A path on a registered Windows Server (e.g., D:\Shares\Sales). A server can have endpoints in multiple sync groups but must be registered to only one Storage Sync Service.
Optional per server endpoint. Volume free space policy and date policy decide which files are tiered to Azure.

howItWorks: Create a file share in a storage account and choose its tier (premium SSD, or standard transaction optimized / hot / cool).
Configure identity-based authentication, assign share-level RBAC roles, and set NTFS ACLs, or mount with the account key for admin access.
For Azure File Sync: deploy a Storage Sync Service, install the agent on each Windows Server, register the servers, create a sync group with the cloud endpoint, then add server endpoints.
Changes on any endpoint sync to the share and from there to other servers. With cloud tiering, cold files become reparse points that recall data on access.
whenToUse: Replace or supplement on-premises file servers and NAS.
Provide shared configuration or storage for multiple VMs or containers (e.g., ACI volumes).
Use Azure File Sync for branch offices that need fast local access with a central cloud copy, or to consolidate file servers.
Use snapshots and soft delete to protect against accidental deletion or ransomware-style changes.
examTips: A sync group has exactly one cloud endpoint; a registered server can belong to only one Storage Sync Service.
Clients can't mount the share over SMB from the internet when port 445 is blocked — the fix is a VPN/ExpressRoute, private endpoint over a private connection, or Azure File Sync.
For per-user share access with AD credentials, enable identity-based auth and assign RBAC share roles; the account key gives superuser access.
Cloud tiering isn't supported on the system (OS) volume.
Snapshot = point-in-time copy to restore files; soft delete = recover a deleted share.
commonMistakes: Expecting NFS shares on standard storage accounts (NFS requires premium file shares).
Registering the same server with two Storage Sync Services.
Adding two cloud endpoints to one sync group.
Relying only on NTFS ACLs without assigning a share-level RBAC role (or default share permission), which blocks access.

confusedWith.name: Blob storage
confusedWith.difference: Blob is object storage accessed via REST; Files is a mountable SMB/NFS file system.

confusedWith.name: Azure Backup for Azure Files
confusedWith.difference: Backup automates and retains share snapshots on a schedule with policies; File Sync is about syncing and caching.

title: Storage Access: Keys, SAS, Stored Access Policies & Firewalls
summary: Authorize access to storage with Entra ID, account keys or shared access signatures, and restrict network access with firewalls, service endpoints and private endpoints.
overview: Every request to Azure Storage must be authorized. The options, from most to least preferred: Microsoft Entra ID with RBAC data roles, user delegation SAS (signed with Entra credentials), service or account SAS signed with an account key, and the account key itself (full access).

A shared access signature (SAS) is a token appended to a URL that grants limited permissions to specific resources for a limited time. A stored access policy, defined on a container, share, queue or table, lets you set or change the constraints of service SAS tokens centrally — and revoke them without rotating keys.

Network rules (the storage firewall) decide which networks can reach the account's public endpoint: selected virtual networks (via service endpoints), public IP ranges, specific resource instances and trusted Microsoft services. Private endpoints give the account a private IP in your VNet.

keyConcepts.definition: Two 512-bit keys with full access to the account. Two keys enable rotation without downtime. Manage and rotate them with Key Vault or a key expiration policy.
Signed with a user delegation key obtained via Entra ID. Blob/Data Lake only. Recommended SAS type.
Signed with an account key; grants access to resources in one service (blob, file, queue or table). Can be tied to a stored access policy.
Signed with an account key; can grant access across multiple services and to service-level operations.
Defined on a container/share/queue/table. Up to five per resource. Changing or deleting it immediately affects every service SAS that references it.
When set to deny, only allowed VNets, IP ranges, resource instances and trusted services can reach the public endpoint.
Blocks requests authorized with account keys, including account and service SAS; only Entra ID (and user delegation SAS) work.

howItWorks: Prefer Entra ID: assign data roles such as Storage Blob Data Contributor to users, groups or managed identities.
When a client can't use Entra ID, issue a SAS with minimal permissions, a short expiry, HTTPS-only and optionally an allowed IP range.
To be able to revoke service SAS tokens, create them against a stored access policy; delete or edit the policy to revoke or change them.
To revoke SAS signed with a key and not tied to a policy, rotate (regenerate) that key — which invalidates every SAS signed with it.
Lock down network access: set the firewall to selected networks, add VNet subnets (with Microsoft.Storage service endpoint) or IP ranges, or use private endpoints and disable public access.
whenToUse: Entra ID + RBAC for users and Azure-hosted apps (managed identities).
User delegation SAS for giving time-limited access to blobs to external clients.
Stored access policies when you may need to revoke or extend many SAS tokens later.
Firewall + service endpoints when only certain VNets should reach the account; private endpoints when traffic must stay private and public access should be disabled.
examTips: 'Revoke a SAS without affecting other apps' → it must reference a stored access policy; delete or modify that policy. Otherwise you'd have to regenerate the key, affecting everything using it.
Stored access policies work with service SAS, not account SAS or user delegation SAS.
Storage firewall IP rules accept public IP addresses only — private (RFC 1918) ranges can't be used; use VNet rules for traffic from VNets.
Allowing a VNet subnet in the firewall requires the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on that subnet.
Rotate keys one at a time: switch apps to key2, regenerate key1, switch back.
Disabling shared key authorization breaks account/service SAS and key-based tools.
commonMistakes: Granting the account key to an app that only needs read access to one container.
Trying to add a private IP range to the storage firewall.
Forgetting that regenerating a key invalidates all SAS tokens signed with it.
Issuing long-lived SAS tokens without a stored access policy.

confusedWith.name: Service endpoint vs private endpoint
confusedWith.difference: Service endpoints secure the public endpoint to selected subnets; private endpoints give the account a private IP in your VNet.

confusedWith.name: Azure RBAC control-plane roles
confusedWith.difference: Contributor manages the account (and can list keys); data roles like Storage Blob Data Reader grant data access via Entra ID.
